dialogs.title: Colloquium — Ad forum
dialogs.intro: Quintus is heading to the town square. As usual, haggling over prices will take a while.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Hodie ad forum ambulo. Quis mecum ambulat?
lines.id: I'm walking to the forum today. Who's coming with me?
lines.literal: today to forum-obj walk-I. who with-me walk-he?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Ego, pater! In foro sunt tabernae.
lines.id: Me, Dad! There are shops in the forum.
lines.literal: I, father-call! in forum-in are-they shop-pl.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Et ego! Sed cum Lydia ambulo.
lines.id: Me too! But I'm walking with Lydia.
lines.literal: and I! but with Lydia-with walk-I.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: She's in the house, with Mom.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.id: We're not going without Lydia. We'll wait.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Dad, why are we going to the forum?

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: In foro frumentum paro. Et de pretio disputo!
lines.id: I'm getting grain at the forum. And arguing about the price!
lines.literal: in forum-in grain-obj prepare-I. and about price-about argue-I!

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: Dad always argues about the price!

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Look, Sextus is walking out of the garden!

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Bene. Cum Sexto semper laeti sumus.
lines.id: Good. We're always happy with Sextus around.
lines.literal: well. with Sextus-with always happy-pl are-we.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Ad forum, ad forum! In forum intramus!
lines.id: To the forum, to the forum! We're going into the forum!
lines.literal: to forum-obj, to forum-obj! into forum-obj enter-we!

notes: **In foro and in forum aren't the same.** *In foro* means "in the forum", with no movement. *In forum* means "into the forum", moving inside. The preposition is the same; the noun's form makes the difference. English uses "in" and "into" to do the same job.

**Mecum, not cum me.** The preposition *cum* sticks to the end of pronouns: *mecum* (with me), *tecum* (with you), *nobiscum* (with us), *vobiscum* (with you all). This reversed order froze in ancient times and can still be heard today in the church phrase *Dominus vobiscum*.

**In villa — notice it looks exactly like the subject form.** This is a quirk of the first declension: the subject form and the "with/in" form are both written *villa*. Romans told them apart by the length of the final vowel, which they never wrote. You tell them apart by the preposition: if *in*, *cum*, *sine*, *ex* or *de* comes before it, it's the "with/in" form.

**De pretio disputat.** *De* means "about" and also "down from". That's where *describe* (write about) and *deduce* (lead down) come from. Latin prepositions almost always have two lives: one about space, one figurative.

blocks.text: This form — called the ablative — is the most versatile form in Latin. It expresses place, means, company, manner, cause and time all at once. Luckily its endings are simple.

So there are only two endings to learn: *-a* for the first group, *-o* for the second. Compare them with the "of" form (*-ae* and *-i*) and the object form (*-am* and *-um*), and you already hold four of the six forms there are.

blocks.title: The four forms you already have
items: **subject**: puella · hortus · templum — who does it, or what is named
**object**: puellam · hortum · templum — what the action is done to
**with/in**: puella · horto · templo — place, means, company, manner
Still to come: the **"to"** form, in Unit 9. After that the list is complete and doesn't grow again until the end of the book.

blocks.text: Latin prepositions choose the form that follows them, and that choice is non-negotiable. Most take the "with/in" form; a small group takes the object form.

head: Preposition
Followed by
Meaning
Example
rows: ex horto — out of the garden

blocks.text: *Ex* and *ab* shorten to *e* and *a* before words starting with a consonant: *ex horto* but *e villa*; *ab amico* but *a villa*. It's purely about sound, just like English *an apple* but *a pear*.

blocks.title: Prepositions you already use every day
items: If you're unsure what a Latin preposition means, think of an English word that contains it. The meaning is almost always still there.

blocks.text: Two prepositions — *in* and *sub* — can be followed by two different forms, and the choice changes the meaning. The rule fits in one sentence: if there is movement, use the object form; if not, use the "with/in" form.

he carries it into the garden

blocks.text: For names of cities and small islands, Latin drops the preposition entirely. The form for "in that city" happens to match the "of" form for cities ending in *-a* and *-us*; linguists call it the locative.

This rule applies only to names of cities, small islands, and three frozen words: *domus*, *rus*, *humus*. For every other place — countries, mountains, rivers — the preposition is used as usual: *in Italia*, *ad silvam*.
